paragraphs.heading: A scar under Mexico
paragraphs.text: The Chicxulub crater is an impact crater hidden beneath the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico, named after the inland town of Chicxulub Pueblo. It formed slightly over 66 million years ago, when an asteroid about ten kilometers wide hit Earth. The crater is thought to be some two hundred kilometers across, and it now lies about a kilometer down, covered by younger sedimentary rock. Along with the much older Sudbury and Vredefort structures, it ranks among the largest impact structures on the planet.

paragraphs.heading: The end of the dinosaurs
paragraphs.text: The impact happened at the same time as the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary, often called the K–Pg boundary. Most scientists now accept that the destruction and climate upheaval it caused were the main reason for the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction. That event wiped out 75% of plant and animal species on Earth, among them every dinosaur except the birds. Signs that the crater came from an impact include shocked quartz, a gravity anomaly and tektites in the areas around it.

paragraphs.heading: A clue in a layer of clay
paragraphs.text: In the late 1970s the geologist Walter Alvarez and his father, the Nobel Prize winner Luis Walter Alvarez, proposed that an impact caused the extinction. Their main evidence was a thin clay layer at the K–Pg boundary in Gubbio, Italy. It held an unusually high level of iridium, an element that is rare on Earth but common in asteroids, up to 160 times the normal background. The idea was that the impactor vaporized, its iridium spread through the atmosphere, and it then settled over Earth's surface with other debris to form the iridium-rich clay.

paragraphs.heading: Doubters and a missing crater
paragraphs.text: Many paleontologists rejected the impact idea at first. They pointed to the lack of fossils close to the boundary, known as the "three-meter problem", as a sign that species had died off gradually. Still, reports of similar iridium spikes at the boundary came in from around the globe, and more than 2,000 papers on the topic appeared in the 1980s. No known crater had the right age and size, so a search began. Alvarez and others looked in the oceans, misled by a wrong reading of glassy spherules that seemed to show the impactor had fallen into open water.

paragraphs.heading: Found by oil hunters
paragraphs.text: In 1978 the geophysicists Glen Penfield and Antonio Camargo were working for Pemex, Mexico's state oil company, on an airborne magnetic survey of the Gulf of Mexico north of the Yucatán. When Penfield laid the magnetic anomalies over gravity maps, he saw a shallow "bullseye" 180 km across standing out from flat, non-magnetic surroundings, which to him clearly marked an impact. Pemex rejected the idea and favored a volcanic explanation. The two men were allowed to present their results at a 1981 geophysics conference, but few people came, because many crater and K–Pg experts were at a different meeting in Snowbird, Utah, that year.

paragraphs.heading: Lost rocks, then proof
paragraphs.text: Penfield had plenty of geophysical data but no rock cores or other physical proof. A well drilled in 1951 had struck a thick layer of andesite about 1.3 kilometers down, which could have come from the heat and pressure of an impact but was written off at the time as a lava dome. Penfield tried to get those samples, but was told they had been lost or destroyed, and he eventually gave up. Later, after getting in touch with Alan R. Hildebrand in 1990, he obtained samples that pointed to an impact.
